plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to open a demat and trading account with a SEBI-registered broker, place a limit order for 1 share of a Nifty 50 company, read its price, market cap and P/E on a quote page, explain in one line why its price moved that day, and work out the tax you'd owe if you sold it.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14: you could compare two companies in the same sector using five numbers and say which you'd rather own and why.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28: you could have a written monthly plan splitting money between an index fund SIP and single shares, and one month of sticking to it.

picture.name: One big organised bazaar
picture.line: The Indian stock market is one huge organised bazaar: each company is a shop, a share is a tiny slice of ownership in one shop, and SEBI is the inspector who keeps the stalls honest.

chapters.title: A share is a slice of a shop
chapters.covers: What you actually own when you buy 1 share, and why its price moves every second: more buyers than sellers pushes it up, more sellers than buyers pushes it down.
chapters.outcome: You can explain in one line why a share's price rose or fell today using buyers and sellers, not headlines.
chapters.hook: Buy one share of a company and you legally own part of it. How much?

chapters.title: The two bazaars and their price boards
chapters.covers: NSE and BSE are the two exchanges (the market buildings), open 9:15 am to 3:30 pm Monday to Friday; Nifty 50 and Sensex are price boards for the 50 and 30 biggest shops; SEBI is the inspector.
chapters.outcome: You can read 'Nifty closed 0.8% down' and say what it does and does not tell you about the 50 companies behind it.
chapters.hook: India has two bazaars selling the same slices. Why is the price almost identical?

chapters.title: Your three accounts
chapters.covers: Bank account holds your money, trading account places orders through a broker, demat account is the locker (with NSDL or CDSL) that holds your shares; what KYC with PAN and Aadhaar means and what a broker charges.
chapters.outcome: You can open a demat and trading account and say which account holds your shares and which holds your cash.
chapters.hook: Your shares don't live with your broker. They sit in a locker most people never name.

chapters.title: Placing your first order
chapters.covers: Market order (buy now at any price) versus limit order (buy only at your price or better), choosing quantity, T+1 settlement meaning shares land the next working day, and the charges on one trade.
chapters.outcome: You can buy 1 share with a limit order, say when it lands in your demat, and list the charges you paid.
chapters.hook: Two orders for the same share at the same minute can pay different prices. Why?

chapters.title: Reading a shop in five numbers
chapters.covers: Price, market cap (price times all shares, so the size of the shop), P/E (price divided by yearly profit per share, so how many years of profit you pay for), 52-week high and low, and dividend yield.
chapters.outcome: You can look at a quote page and say whether a company is large or small, and whether it is priced high or low against its profit.
chapters.hook: 'The market fell today' describes 50 companies, not the thousands listed.

chapters.title: Buying the whole bazaar at once
chapters.covers: Index funds buy all 50 Nifty shops in one go; mutual funds hire a shopper to pick for you; SIP means a fixed amount every month; expense ratio is the yearly fee taken from your money.
chapters.outcome: You can set up a monthly SIP in a Nifty 50 index fund and say what expense ratio you are paying.
chapters.hook: You can own all 50 Nifty companies with ₹500 a month. How?

chapters.title: The toll on the way out, and the traps
chapters.covers: Tax on listed shares: held under 12 months is taxed at 20%, held over 12 months at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year; why to refuse stock tips, and why SEBI's 2023 study found 9 in 10 individual futures and options traders lost money.
chapters.outcome: You can work out the tax on a sale you are planning and name three things you will say no to in your first year.
chapters.hook: The WhatsApp 'sure-shot' tip is banned by SEBI. Here's how to spot one.

hooksFrom.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to open a demat and trading account with a SEBI-registered broker, place a limit order for one share and read what happened to it, explain a 'Nifty fell 1%' headline in plain words, start a monthly SIP into an index fund, and say which side of the 12-month line your tax falls on.
hooksFrom.horizon14: Later, by day 14: open a company's quarterly results and say whether its profit grew, without anyone's help.
hooksFrom.horizon28: Later, by day 28: hold one index fund plus two or three shares you chose for reasons you can write down in a sentence each.

picture.name: A slice of a chai stall
picture.line: Every share is one slice of a chai stall, and the stock market is the bazaar where those slices change hands all day.

chapters.title: What you actually own when you buy a share
chapters.covers: A share as one slice of a company, why a company sells slices in the first place, and where a share's price comes from: whatever the last buyer agreed to pay.
chapters.outcome: You can explain what you own after buying one share of a company and why its price changes before you've done anything.
chapters.hook: Buy one share of a company and you legally own part of it. How much?

chapters.title: The two bazaars and the referee
chapters.covers: NSE and BSE as the two places slices trade, SEBI as the regulator that polices them, and market hours of 9:15 am to 3:30 pm on weekdays.
chapters.outcome: You can name the two exchanges, say who polices them, and say when you can and cannot buy.
chapters.hook: India has two bazaars selling the same slices. Why is the price almost identical?

chapters.title: Your three accounts and the runner
chapters.covers: Bank, demat and trading accounts and what each one does, the broker as your runner into the bazaar, how to open an account, and the fees you'll actually pay.
chapters.outcome: You can open an account with a SEBI-registered broker and say what every fee on the statement is for.
chapters.hook: Your shares don't live with your broker. They sit in a locker most people never name.

chapters.title: Placing your first order
chapters.covers: Reading the quote screen (buyer price, seller price, day's high and low, volume), market order versus limit order, and T+1: the share lands in your demat the next working day.
chapters.outcome: You can place a limit order for one share and read what the screen shows the next day.
chapters.hook: Two orders for the same share at the same minute can pay different prices. Why?

chapters.title: Reading the price board
chapters.covers: Nifty 50 (50 big NSE companies) and Sensex (30 big BSE companies) as the bazaar's price board, what 'the market is up' means, and the three things that move prices: profits, news, and crowd mood.
chapters.outcome: You can read 'Nifty fell 1%' in the news and say what moved, what didn't, and whether your share is in it.
chapters.hook: 'The market fell today' describes 50 companies, not the thousands listed.

chapters.title: Buying the whole bazaar at once
chapters.covers: Mutual funds and index funds as paying a manager to hold many slices, SIP (a fixed monthly buy), expense ratio as the yearly fee, and direct versus regular plans.
chapters.outcome: You can set up a monthly SIP into an index fund and say exactly what you're paying for it each year.
chapters.hook: You can own all 50 Nifty companies with ₹500 a month. How?

chapters.title: Staying safe: risk, tax and tips
chapters.covers: Why a stall can close, spreading money across slices, the 12-month line that splits short-term and long-term tax, how to spot a stock-tip scam, and three rules to write before you buy.
chapters.outcome: You can explain the 12-month tax line, spot an unregistered tip, and write your own three buying rules.
chapters.hook: The WhatsApp 'sure-shot' tip is banned by SEBI. Here's how to spot one.
